read.sections.0.heading.source: Ask three questions before you share
read.sections.0.heading.back: Ask three questions before you share

read.sections.0.text.source: Messages can spread very quickly, and a shocking story often travels fastest. In Brightwater, a page called Brightwater Daily Truth posted that the town bridge would close for a whole year. It said, “Share this before they delete it.” Words like these push people to hurry, and hurrying makes it easy to share something false. Before you share, ask three questions. Who is behind the information? What is the evidence? What do other sources say? The Brightwater post gives no names, no evidence and no link to the town council, which looks after the bridge.
read.sections.0.text.back: Messages can spread very quickly, and a shocking story often spreads fastest. In Brightwater, a page named Brightwater Daily Truth posted that the town bridge would close for a whole year. The post said, “Share this before they delete it.” Words like these push people to hurry, and when we hurry, we easily share something false. Before you share, ask three questions. Who is behind the information? What evidence is there? What do other sources say? The Brightwater post gives no names, no evidence and no link to the town council, the party that looks after the bridge.

read.sections.1.text.source: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people judge real websites about social issues. There were 10 historians who teach at universities, 10 professional fact-checkers from news organisations and 25 Stanford students. In one task, they compared the websites of two doctors' groups that gave advice about bullying. Most historians thought both sites were reliable. The fact-checkers quickly left each page and opened other sources to find out who was behind it. This is called lateral reading, which means reading sideways across many sources instead of down one page. The fact-checkers reached better answers in much less time. The researchers chose a small group on purpose, so the study shows how these experts worked, not how everyone reads.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people judge real websites about social issues. There were 10 historians who teach at universities, 10 professional fact-checkers from news organisations and 25 Stanford students. In one task, they compared the websites of two doctors' groups that gave advice about bullying. Most historians thought both sites could be trusted. The fact-checkers, though, quickly left each page and opened other sources to find out who was behind it. This is called lateral reading, which means reading sideways across many sources, not reading down one page. The fact-checkers reached better answers in much less time. The researchers deliberately chose a small group of people, so this study shows how these experts worked, not how everyone reads.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people check real websites. There were 10 historians who teach at universities. The fact-checkers left each page fast. They opened other sources to find out who made it. This is called lateral reading. It means reading sideways. The fact-checkers got better answers, faster. The group was small, so the study shows how these experts worked. It does not show how everyone reads.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people check real websites. There were 10 historians who teach at universities. The fact-checkers got better answers, more quickly. The group was small, so this study shows how these experts worked. It does not show how everyone reads.

read.sections.2.text.source: Agreement helps only when sources have their own evidence. Several websites can repeat the same claim because they all copied one post, and ten copies are still only one source. The town council looks after the bridge, so it knows the dates: two days of repairs, not a whole year. The radio and the fact-checkers asked the council and say the same. The chat page only copied the first post word for word, so it adds no evidence. So the first post is false. Don't share it; share the council's notice instead. Sometimes you can't check a claim, for example with no internet. Then ask a teacher or wait. News can change, so check again later, for example if the repairs take longer.
read.sections.2.text.back: Agreement only helps when each source has its own evidence. Several websites can repeat the same claim because they all copied one post, and ten copies are still only one source. The town council looks after the bridge, so the council knows the dates: two days of repair work, not a whole year. The radio and the fact-checkers asked the council and say the same thing. The chat page only copied the first post word for word, so it adds no evidence. So the first post is false. Don't share it; share the council's notice instead. Sometimes you cannot check a claim, for example when there is no internet. If so, ask a teacher or wait. News can change, so check again later, for example if the repair work takes longer.

watch.summary.source: This short video explains lateral reading. It is a way to check information that professional fact-checkers use. Many people check a website by reading down the page. They look at how it looks and what it says about itself. But a page can look serious and still give false or one-sided information. Fact-checkers do something different. After a quick look, they leave the page. They open new pages and search for what other sources say about it and about who is behind it. By reading less of the page and more about it, they learn more, and they learn it faster. You can do the same thing. Before you trust a page, find out who made it and what others say about it.
watch.summary.back: This short video explains lateral reading. This is a way of checking information that professional fact-checkers use. Many people check a website by reading down the page. They look at how it looks and what it says about itself. But a page can look serious but still give false or one-sided information. Fact-checkers do something different. After a quick look, they leave the page. They open new pages and look for what other sources say about that page and about who is behind it. By reading less of the page and more about it, they learn more, and more quickly. You can also do the same thing. Before you trust a page, find out who made it and what other people say about it.

educatorNotes.1.source: The research in section 2 is Wineburg and McGrew (Stanford History Education Group working paper, 2017; a shortened version in Teachers College Record, 2018–19). The 45 participants, chosen on purpose rather than at random, were 10 PhD historians teaching at universities in California and Washington, 10 professional fact-checkers at news and fact-checking organisations and 25 Stanford undergraduates. They judged live websites and searched the web on social and political issues: for example, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the much smaller American College of Pediatricians on bullying (most historians thought both reliable; most students rated the second more reliable), and who paid for a teacher-tenure lawsuit. The authors note the small samples and timed tasks. The group became the independent Digital Inquiry Group in January 2024.
educatorNotes.1.back: The research in part 2 is Wineburg and McGrew (Stanford History Education Group working paper, 2017; a short version in Teachers College Record, 2018–19). The 45 participants, chosen deliberately and not at random, were 10 historians with PhDs teaching at universities in California and Washington, 10 professional fact-checkers at news and fact-checking organisations, and 25 undergraduate students at Stanford. They judged real websites and searched the web on social and political issues: for example, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the much smaller American College of Pediatricians on bullying (most historians thought both could be trusted; most students rated the second as more trustworthy), and who paid for a lawsuit about teachers' permanent posts. The authors note that the samples were small and the tasks timed. The group became the independent Digital Inquiry Group in January 2024.
educatorNotes.1.note: "Teacher-tenure lawsuit" is "tuntutan mahkamah tentang jawatan tetap guru" (lawsuit about teachers' permanent posts); check it reads clearly to Malaysian teachers.

educatorNotes.2.source: Lateral reading normally needs the internet. On an offline device the activity's source cards stand in for new pages, and the print view lists them for work on paper; a teacher can also play “the other sources”. The evidence shows only the post, so learners meet the other sources in the activity. Write and Speak use what the learner found there rather than repeat the check. In Indonesia, Mafindo recommends fact-checking sites such as TurnBackHoax and CekFakta (Liputan6, 2026).
